data: This page describes the design. Where a part is not written yet it says planned.
data.processes#Processes: With the engine’s WASI host (wctrd --wasi engine, the default), a guest can start other programs of its container through a small subset of WASIX, in WASIX’s own import module wasix_32v1: proc_spawn2, proc_spawn3, proc_join, proc_id, proc_parent, fd_pipe, tty_get and tty_set (no fork, exec, threads or signals), since engine v0.17.0. A child is a new instance of a module of the same root filesystem; a container’s processes form one group (at most 64 at once, 32 spawns per second), killed together with the container. This is what runs sh and its pipelines (the shell), shell-form RUN in a build, and wctr exec (engine v0.20.0).
data.published-ports#Published ports: A container has no socket on the host, so a published port (run -p, engine v0.22.0) is a listener that wctrd opens on the host and proxies into the container’s network endpoint. It listens on 127.0.0.1 unless the binding names an address. See Networking.
data.the-command-line-wctr#The command line,: The client. It finds the daemon at /var/run/wctr.sock, or at the address in the WCTR_HOST environment variable. Because the API is Docker-Engine compatible, other clients of that API can talk to wctrd as well; wctr is the command the labs teach.
data.the-daemon-wctrd#The daemon, wctrd: A Go program, pure Go, no cgo. It owns the images, the containers and their state, and serves an HTTP API on the Unix socket /var/run/wctr.sock. The API is compatible with the Docker Engine API: the reference it is written against is Docker Engine API v1.47, and the subset M1 covers is the one the commands pull, run, ps, logs, rm, rmi, inspect and images need: GET /_ping, POST /images/create, the image list and delete endpoints, and the container create, start, list, inspect, logs, wait and delete endpoints. Logs of a container without a TTY use the API’s multiplexed stream framing.
data.the-executors#The executors:
An executor runs one module with a root filesystem, arguments, an environment and a working directory.
wazero (released in v0.1.0): the native executor. wazero is a pure-Go WebAssembly runtime with a WASI preview1 implementation, so the engine stays a single static binary. The container’s root filesystem is adapted to wazero’s writable filesystem interface; the image’s WorkingDir is passed as PWD, which is where a Go wasip1 program takes its initial directory from. Browser (runtime/browser, engine v0.2.0): the same executor contract implemented over the browser’s WebAssembly, with the WASI host shared with the native side (wasi) and the API served in-process (api/inproc), so the playground needs no server that runs containers.
data.the-images#The images:
An image is an OCI image whose manifest or index entry has os=wasip1 and arch=wasm. The engine pulls from an OCI registry (the Distribution API, with the registry’s bearer-token authentication), selects the wasip1/wasm entry of an index, verifies digests, and unpacks the layers in order — whiteouts included — into the container’s root filesystem. The Wasm OCI artifact layout of the CNCF TAG-Runtime (application/wasm layer, application/vnd.wasm.config.v0+json config) is also read.
Images are meant to be apt-like: a small base plus the tools a lab needs, built from pkgx wasip1 bottles. go-pkgx is gaining a wasip1/wasm target for this; until it ships, images come from whatever registry holds wasip1 images.
data.the-pieces#The pieces: wctr CLI ──► /var/run/wctr.sock ──► wctrd ──► executor ──► a wasip1 module (Docker Engine API) │ │ │ ├─ native: wazero (v0.1.0) │ └─ browser: runtime/browser (v0.2.0) └─ image store, root filesystem
data.what-is-not-in-this-design-yet#What is n: A mini-Kubernetes is on the roadmap and does not exist. Published ports in the browser (in progress) and exec in the playground (the browser executor has it since engine v0.26.0; the playground is not rebuilt yet) are also still to come: see Limitations.

data:
wctr build builds OCI images from a Containerfile (or a Dockerfile, same syntax) for the engine. It is the separate module go-wasmcontainers/build (v0.4.0), which drives the engine through its API, the way BuildKit sits beside a container daemon: each step runs in a container made from the previous step’s image, which is then committed. Pure Go, so it also runs in the browser.
wctr build is built into wctr since cmd/wctr v0.1.0 (see Getting started); the standalone wctr-build still exists. It needs a wctrd of v0.12.0 or later, and v0.17.0 or later for shell-form RUN.
$ wctr build -t lab/app:v1 . $ wctr run --rm lab/app:v1
data.cache#Cache: A step is reused when its parent image, the configuration it produces, the instruction and the digest of its inputs are the same. The cache is kept in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/wasmcontainers/build-cache.json (in memory in a browser).
data.flags#Flags:
wctr build [OPTIONS] PATH | -
Flag -t, --tag NAME[:TAG] name the image (repeatable) -f, --file FILE the Containerfile (-: standard input); default PATH/Containerfile, else PATH/Dockerfile --build-arg K=V a build argument (K alone: from the environment) --target STAGE build up to this stage --no-cache run every step --progress plain plain progress, the only kind -q, --quiet print only the image ID PATH is the build context, sent without what its .containerignore (else .dockerignore) excludes; - reads the context as a tar on standard input. Multi-stage builds work.
data.speed#Speed: A seven-instruction build with one RUN took 61.7 ms cold and 4.8 ms with every step cached (build v0.2.0). Measured under heavy load (a load average of 66), so indicative only, and not yet compared with BuildKit.
data.what-works-and-what-does-not-yet#What wo: Exec-form RUN ["prog", "arg"] works: it runs a WebAssembly program in the step’s container. Shell-form RUN cmd works on an image with a shell (build v0.3.0). It runs /bin/sh through the engine’s WASIX process subset (engine v0.17.0 or later), so pipes, redirections, && and command substitution work, with coreutils on the shell base image (wctr pull ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell:0.1.0, public). In an image without a runnable shell the build stops with a precise error. A step’s output streams as the step runs (build v0.4.0), instead of being printed when it ends. Not supported, each a precise error and never ignored: here-documents, RUN --mount, ADD from a URL or Git, COPY --parents/--exclude, --chown by name, symbolic --chmod, and xz/zstd archives in ADD.

data.bounds-on-untrusted-content#Bounds on un: What Bound blob 512 MiB image 1 GiB, 128 layers unpacked layers 1 GiB, 131072 files gzip expansion ratio 200:1 logs kept 8 MiB per container
data.events-v060#Events (v0.6.0): wctr events and GET /events stream NDJSON. --since and --until bound the range, and the filters are type, event, container, image, volume, network and label. The last 1024 events are kept, and a reader that is too slow is cut off.
data.exit-status-of-wctr-run#Exit status of w:
The container’s own, or:
Code Meaning 125 the CLI or the daemon failed 126 not a WebAssembly module 127 module not found 134 the module trapped 137 killed, or the wall-clock timeout
data.for-builders-v0120-api-only-for-now#For: POST /images/load takes an OCI image layout as a tar; each index.json entry is named by io.containerd.image.name or org.opencontainers.image.ref.name, else . It is checked as a pull is, and nothing is read from the host. PUT /containers/{id}/archive?path=DIR extracts a tar into a container (relative clean names only, no devices, paths resolved inside the container, its quota applies), and GET returns a tar of a path. These two routes accept uploads up to 1 GiB by default; every other request is limited to 1 MiB. GET /images/{name}/json shows the full image config, the history, and RootFS.Layers as diff_ids. Dangling images appear as . HEAD on the archive route returns only the path’s stat, without building a tar (v0.14.0). The Go client filters lists through ContainersFiltered, NetworksFiltered and VolumesFiltered, which take an api.Filters. v0.18.0 had changed the signatures of Containers, Networks and Volumes to take filters, which broke the dashboard; v0.21.0 restored them, and a new CI job compiles downstream modules against the engine. A start refused before the process exists (a port, a network, a volume) is recorded as an exit with code 128 and the reason, as Docker records it: a run --rm returns at once and its container is removed (v0.22.0). Since v0.23.0, wctr run exits 125 when the daemon refuses the start. Other modules add commands to wctr through an extension hook, cli.Options.Extra; wctr build and wctr compose use it. wctr build needs a wctrd of v0.12.0 or later (v0.17.0 for shell-form RUN).
data.health-checks#Health checks:
run --health-cmd CMD, --health-interval, --health-timeout, --health-start-period, --health-start-interval, --health-retries and --no-healthcheck (engine v0.28.0), as well as an image’s HEALTHCHECK and Config.Healthcheck. The test (CMD argv, CMD-SHELL through /bin/sh -c, or NONE) runs inside the running container through the exec machinery, every interval (default 30 s; 5 s during the start period), and is killed after the timeout (default 30 s, exit code −1). A pass makes the container healthy; retries consecutive failures (default 3) make it unhealthy; failures in the start period do not count. Fields left empty are taken from the image’s check. inspect shows State.Health (Status, FailingStreak, and the last 5 results with at most 4 KiB of output each), ps shows Up … (healthy), and each change of status is a health_status event (healthy or unhealthy; --filter event=health_status). Probes stop with the container and are not exec events. Unlike Docker, an interval or timeout below 100 ms is refused. A CMD-SHELL probe needs a /bin/sh in the image (the shell image has one).
For embedders. An in-process engine must register wasi.WASIX in its HostModules, as wctrd does, to run the shell image or health checks.
data.persistence-v040#Persistence (v0.4.0): Containers survive a wctrd restart: they are kept under --data-root in containers/ (state, exit code, logs and written files). A container that was running comes back exited with code 137, and a --rm container is removed. An entry that is corrupted is dropped and reported.
data.restart-policies#Restart policies:
run --restart and HostConfig.RestartPolicy (engine v0.25.0), as Docker’s:
always restarts a container whenever it exits, and starts it with the engine; unless-stopped does the same, except that the engine leaves it stopped if a user stopped it; on-failure[:N] restarts it when it exits with a code other than 0, at most N times (0: no bound); no is the default. A user’s stop or kill ends the policy until the next start, which counts from zero. Each restart waits first: 100 ms, doubled after every run shorter than 10 s, at most a minute. Meanwhile the container is restarting: ps lists it as Restarting (code) … ago, and rm needs -f. A start the engine refuses (a volume, a network, a port) is not retried. inspect shows HostConfig.RestartPolicy, RestartCount and State.Restarting. A policy cannot be combined with --rm.
data.stats-v070#Stats (v0.7.0): wctr stats and the stats endpoint report memory against its limit, bytes written, layer and log size, and pids. CPU is not measured: a WebAssembly guest gives no CPU accounting, so it is shown as --.
data.terminals-and-input-v0300#Terminals and:
wctr run -i/-t, wctr attach and wctr start -ai give a container’s first process its own stdin and terminal. They use Docker’s fields Config.Tty, Config.OpenStdin, Config.StdinOnce and HostConfig.ConsoleSize.
A container’s first process can get a stdin that attached clients write into. With -t it also gets a terminal: the engine handles line editing, echo and CR LF, and keeps keys typed ahead when a program switches to raw mode (the hand-over of the typed line is engine v0.29.2). POST /containers/{id}/attach accepts stdin=1 and detachKeys. Like exec start, it does not hijack the connection: the request body carries stdin and the response streams the output. POST /containers/{id}/resize is new. Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q detaches; detach keys use Docker’s format. It works in both executors, the native one and the browser’s. No host call blocks on stdin (v0.29.1). wctr as go install gives it (cmd/wctr v0.2.0) requires engine v0.22.0, so these commands are in engine v0.30.0’s cli package and reach wctr when cmd/wctr requires it; the daemon (wctrd v0.30.0) serves the API.
data.volumes-v080#Volumes (v0.8.0): wctr volume create|ls|inspect|rm|prune, and wctr run -v NAME:/path[:ro]. Only named volumes exist: a host path is refused. A volume is shared between containers, :ro is enforced, and volumes survive a restart and a page reload. They appear in system df and in inspect.
data.wctr#wctr:
The client. It finds the daemon at -H unix:///path, else $WCTR_HOST, else unix:///var/run/wctr.sock.
Command Flags pull IMAGE IMAGE is a registry reference or oci:[:] images -q run IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARG...] --rm, -d/--detach, --name, -e/--env KEY=value (or KEY from the shell), --entrypoint, -w/--workdir, -m/--memory, -v NAME:/path[:ro] (v0.8.0), --network NAME (v0.10.0), --network-alias NAME (v0.14.0), --gpu (v0.13.0), -p/--publish [ip:][hostPort:]containerPort[/tcp|udp] (the ip defaults to 127.0.0.1), -P/--publish-all, --expose PORT[/proto] (v0.22.0), --restart no|always|unless-stopped|on-failure[:N] (v0.25.0; not with --rm; see Restart policies), --health-cmd and the other --health-* flags, --no-healthcheck (v0.28.0), -i/--interactive, -t/--tty, --detach-keys (v0.30.0; see “Terminals and input” below) attach [--no-stdin] [--detach-keys K] CONTAINER this terminal to a running container: its output, and its input if it was created with -i; Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q detaches and leaves it running; exits with its status when it stops (v0.30.0) port CONTAINER [PRIVATE_PORT[/PROTO]] where a running container’s ports are published, e.g. 80/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8080 (v0.22.0) ps -a/--all, -q; a PORTS column as Docker writes it (v0.22.0) logs CONTAINER -f/--follow rm CONTAINER... -f/--force rmi IMAGE... -f/--force commit CONTAINER [REPO[:TAG]] -m/--message, -a/--author, -c/--change (CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, EXPOSE, LABEL, ONBUILD, STOPSIGNAL, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR): the container’s changes as one OCI layer on the parent’s, with a history entry; without a name, a image addressable by ID (v0.12.0) tag SOURCE TARGET another name for an image; a tag that moves leaves the old image as (v0.12.0) inspect NAME|ID... containers, then images build, compose wctr build and wctr compose, built into wctr since cmd/wctr v0.1.0; they use wctr’s -H, which goes before the subcommand exec [-d] [-i] [-t] [-e K=V] [-w DIR] CONTAINER CMD... a further process in a running container, in its process group; needs --wasi engine; exits with the command’s status; -t gives it a terminal (the engine does the line editing and echo); -u accepts only root or 0 (engine v0.20.0). In the browser executor since v0.26.0: the process runs in its own worker inside the container’s process group, counts against its limits and is killed with it. -t follows window resizes since v0.27.0: SIGWINCH on unix, a 2 Hz size sampling on Windows, wasip1 and js kill CONTAINER... start CONTAINER... -a/--attach (one container: prints this run’s output and exits with its status) and -i (also sends this terminal’s input, for a container created with -i) (v0.30.0); -a/--all (v0.5.0) stop CONTAINER... -t, accepted and ignored (v0.5.0) restart CONTAINER... -t, accepted and ignored (v0.5.0) diff CONTAINER (v0.4.0) events --since, --until, filters on type, event, container, image, volume and label (v0.6.0) stats (v0.7.0) volume create|ls|inspect|rm|prune (v0.8.0) network create|ls|inspect|rm (v0.10.0) network connect [--alias NAME] NETWORK CONTAINER a running container at once (v0.14.0) network disconnect [-f] NETWORK CONTAINER (v0.14.0) network prune [-f] [--filter label=K[=V]] unused networks (v0.14.0) system df -v (v0.4.0) system prune -a, -f (v0.4.0) version completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell prints the completion script for that shell (v0.3.0) wctr run pulls an image it does not have.
A WebAssembly guest has no signals, so wctr stop kills the container at once: -t is accepted for compatibility and ignored. In the API, /attach is a plain streamed response, not a hijacked connection.
data.wctrd#wctrd: Flag Meaning Default -H, --host unix:///path the socket to serve (unix only; TCP is refused, the API has no authentication) unix:///var/run/wctr.sock --data-root where images are kept $XDG_DATA_HOME/wasmcontainers, else ~/.local/share/wasmcontainers --memory linear-memory limit per container 256m --run-timeout wall-clock limit per run (0 = none) 10m --storage-quota bytes a container may write 256m --max-containers containers at once 256 --insecure-registry host:port allow plain HTTP to that registry (loopback registries are always plain HTTP) none

data: wctr compose runs a multi-container application described by the Compose Specification, through the engine’s API. It is the separate module go-wasmcontainers/compose (v0.6.0, status M1; it needs engine v0.14.0 or later, engine v0.22.0 or later for published ports, engine v0.25.0 or later for restart policies and engine v0.28.0 or later for health checks), and it is built into wctr since cmd/wctr v0.1.0 (see Getting started); the standalone wctr-compose still exists. Compose files are accepted in three formats, YAML, JSON and HCL2, which load to the same model; files of different formats merge (-f compose.yaml -f override.hcl). The HCL2 mapping is specified in docs/HCL.md.
data.commands#Commands:
wctr compose [-f FILE]... [-p NAME] [--profile P]... COMMAND
Command Flags up [SERVICE...] -d, --force-recreate, --build, --remove-orphans, --wait-timeout (how long a service_healthy dependency may stay starting; default 5 minutes) down -v ps [SERVICE...] -a, -q logs [SERVICE...] -f start, stop, restart dependencies first; stop also stops a container waiting to restart, and ends its restart policy until the next start rm [SERVICE...] -s pull, images build builds the services’ images with wctr build config --format yaml|json|hcl, -q, --services Loading is complete: discovery, interpolation, .env, merging, extends, include, profiles, and validation against the specification’s schema, with every error carrying file:line:column. The Compose files are untrusted input and every reader is bounded and fuzzed.
data.health-checks-v060#Health checks (v0.6.0:
A service’s healthcheck is applied, through the engine’s health checks (engine v0.28.0 or later; see Commands): test as CMD, CMD-SHELL or NONE, the durations, and retries. disable: true is NONE. What a healthcheck leaves unset, even test, comes from the image’s own check, which the engine merges field by field, as Docker does. CMD-SHELL needs a /bin/sh in the image, for example ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell (Shell).
depends_on with condition: service_healthy really waits. The wait follows the engine’s events, and up fails when the dependency reports unhealthy (with the last probe’s exit code and output), when it stops first, when it has no health check, and after --wait-timeout (default 5 minutes) when it is still starting. A dependency with required: false that fails any of these is a warning, and up carries on. The engine’s minimum interval is 100 ms.
With this, every engine feature compose waited for is applied: aliases and several networks, label filters, ports, restart policies and health checks.
data.limits#Limits:
What the engine cannot do yet, and compose therefore does not:
Build attributes such as remote contexts, cache_from and secrets are accepted with a warning and not applied; what the builder itself does not do is on the Build page. No host bind mounts, and no file outside the project directory.
data.networking-v030#Networking (v0.3.0): Services reach each other by service name and aliases, on as many networks as they declare. This needs engine v0.14.0 or later (it is built against v0.18.0). Builds (up --build, build) use wctr build (compose v0.2.0).
data.published-ports-v040#Published ports (v0: A service’s ports (short and long syntax) and expose are applied, through the engine’s published ports (engine v0.22.0 or later; see Networking). One difference from the specification, on purpose: a port that names no host address ("8080:80", or the long syntax without host_ip) is published on 127.0.0.1, the engine’s default, not on every interface as the specification says, so that a lab container does not become a service on the machine’s network by accident. Write "0.0.0.0:8080:80" (or host_ip: 0.0.0.0) when that is meant.
data.restart-policies-v050#Restart policies (: A service’s restart (no, always, on-failure[:N], unless-stopped) and deploy.restart_policy are applied, through the engine’s restart policies (engine v0.25.0 or later; see Commands). In deploy.restart_policy, condition none, on-failure and any map to no, on-failure and always, and max_attempts is the retry count. When both are written, deploy.restart_policy wins over restart. delay and window are not applied: the engine’s own backoff (100 ms, doubling up to a minute) applies, and compose warns about them. compose stop also stops a container that is waiting to restart, and ends its restart policy until the next start.

data: A graphical dashboard for the engine — containers, images, volumes, networks and a wctr terminal — built with go-widgets, running in the browser on the same engine and API as wctr. Every action shows the wctr command it stands for. This is dashboard v0.8.0.
data.in-the-playground#In the playground: The dashboard is the playground’s default UI since playground v0.3.0 (Containers, Images, Volumes, Networks, Terminal). The terminal-only page stays at ?ui=terminal.
data.limitations#Limitations: The standalone demo keeps its state in memory: nothing persists across a reload. In the playground the dashboard runs on the persistent engine worker instead. Browsers keep Ctrl-W, Ctrl-T and Ctrl-N, so the terminal cannot use them. dashboard.wasm was 20.45 MB raw and 5.32 MB gzipped when measured. Dashboard v0.4.2 made it smaller (go-widgets toolkit v0.345.1), and no newer figure has been measured.
data.the-terminal-widget#The terminal widget: The terminal in the dashboard is the Terminal widget that go-widgets/toolkit v0.342.0 adds: a subset of xterm, safe for untrusted output. It has no reply channel (nothing the output prints is ever sent back), and OSC, DCS and APC sequences are dropped.
data.what-it-does#What it does: The Start, Stop and Restart buttons use the engine’s /start, /stop and /restart, and show the matching wctr start|stop|restart NAME line in the footer and in the terminal. Stop returns once the container has exited. The status bar shows the storage, from GET /system/df (for example IndexedDB 2MB of 1GB (persistent)). It follows GET /events instead of polling. When the stream drops, it refreshes and reconnects from the last event. The Volumes view shows each volume’s size and use count, and can create, inspect, remove (with force) and prune; each action shows its wctr volume … line. A container’s detail shows its mounts and a Stats tab: a memory gauge against the limit, a sparkline of recent readings, bytes written, log size and pids. CPU is shown as -- because it is not measured. The run dialog accepts -v NAME:/path[:ro]. Networks view and Join class (v0.5.0): the networks, the networks of each container, and a Join class… dialog for a teacher’s relay. Surfaces view (v0.6.0): one pane per GPU surface a container opens (wasi-gfx:surface, rendered by the gpu module in the engine’s worker), titled with the container and the surface number, with its size and frame rate. A closed surface keeps its last frame, greyed, until you dismiss it. Surface input (v0.8.0): a pane forwards pointer events (down, up, move, in surface pixels, scaled from the letterboxed frame; events outside the frame are dropped) and key events (the KeyboardEvent.code, the text when it is one character, the modifiers) to the guest, through gpu v0.6.0’s webgpu.SurfaceInput. A press on a pane’s frame gives it the focus (drawn in the accent colour); only the focused pane sends keys, and it takes every key except F6, which leaves it. Pointer moves are coalesced to one per surface per frame. A closed surface takes no input. The playground (v0.4.1) still uses dashboard v0.6.0. Open shell (v0.7.0): an “Open shell” toolbar action and a Shell tab in a container’s detail, the equivalent of wctr exec -it CONTAINER sh. It starts a TTY exec of /bin/sh at the terminal’s size, sends the keys as raw bytes, follows resizes, and shows the exit code when the shell ends. Request bodies of unknown length are streamed over the bridge, which carries the shell’s stdin. The container’s image needs a /bin/sh. It was tested live in Chromium and Firefox. Live demo: https://go-wasmcontainers.github.io/dashboard/. Source: go-wasmcontainers/dashboard.

data:
A design document decides how a planned part will be built, and why, before its code exists. Each one lists the references it was written against. Nothing in this section has shipped.
Classroom network: how students’ browsers reach each other’s containers through a relay and firewall on the teacher’s laptop, managed through a gRPC control API

Status: M-relay-1 and M-relay-2 shipped in relay v0.1.0, M-relay-2b (the live flow map) in v0.2.0 (see Relay); the rest is planned. The implementation lives in go-wasmcontainers/relay. This page decides what is built and records why, so the code can be reviewed against it. Milestones are named M-relay-1 and up.
data.1-transport-between-the-browser-and-the-:
Three candidates were compared.
WebSocket (wss) WebTransport WebRTC data channels Support every browser the labs target Chrome 97, Firefox 114, Safari 26.4 (iOS 26.4) per MDN’s compatibility data, and serverCertificateHashes from Chrome 100, Firefox 125, Safari 26.4; MDN marks it Baseline 2026 (“since March 2026”) Baseline widely available since January 2020 (MDN) In a Web Worker yes yes (MDN: the constructor is available in workers) not established by MDN (an RTCDataChannel is transferable, which is not the same) Certificate without a public CA must be trusted by the browser serverCertificateHashes: no CA needed, but strict constraints (below) DTLS fingerprints from signalling Multiplexing ours, in the frames native streams and datagrams (QUIC), no head-of-line blocking between streams native channels Firewall sees the traffic yes, it terminates at the relay yes only if forced through the relay, which removes the reason to use it serverCertificateHashes lets a page connect to a server whose certificate no CA signed, by giving the SHA-256 of the certificate. The W3C WebTransport Candidate Recommendation (30 July 2026) and MDN set the constraints:
the certificate must be X.509v3, its total validity period must not exceed two weeks, and the current time must be inside it; the accepted key algorithms are implementation-defined but must include ECDSA P-256 (secp256r1) and must not include RSA; the hash is sha-256, over the DER encoding of the leaf certificate; the option only works on a dedicated connection (allowPooling: false). The relay can meet these: it generates an ECDSA P-256 certificate valid for at most 13 days (a margin under 14) when a class starts, and hands its hash to students in the join link. A class that lasts longer gets a new certificate and a new link.
WebRTC is rejected. Its value is a direct peer-to-peer path; the firewall must see every flow, so the topology would be a star through the relay anyway, and WebRTC would only add ICE, DTLS and SCTP to a connection the relay terminates. It is also not established that it can be used from the Web Worker that runs the engine.
Decision. WebSocket is the first transport because it works in every target browser, in a worker, and through the simplest server code. It carries everything over one TCP connection, so one lost Wi-Fi frame stalls every flow of that browser (head-of-line blocking); WebTransport removes that and is the second transport (M-relay-4), selected per browser by feature detection, with the same framing on its streams.
A page that talks to the teacher’s laptop runs into four browser rules.
Mixed content. An https page cannot open ws://; MDN classes any non-upgradable insecure request as blockable, and the Local Network Access draft states that WebSocket has no RequestInit, so ws:// URLs cannot use its mixed-content exemption either. The relay must speak wss, so it needs a certificate the browser accepts. Local Network Access (formerly Private Network Access). The WICG draft (7 August 2026) classifies addresses as loopback, local (RFC 1918, link-local, fc00::/7) and public; a request from a document to a less public address space needs the local-network permission, only from a secure context. The WebSocket handshake is a fetch, so it is covered; WebTransport inherits the rule through fetch. Chrome’s announcement says the permission prompt launches in Chrome 142, and in June 2025 it still listed WebSocket, WebTransport and WebRTC as not yet gated. The design assumes they are gated: a page on GitHub Pages (public) that opens a socket to 192.168.x.y (local) triggers the prompt, and a school’s enterprise policy may pre-deny it. A page served from the relay itself is in the local address space, so its connections back to the relay are not “less public” and need no permission. Cross-origin isolation. The executor uses SharedArrayBuffer, which MDN allows only in a secure context that is cross-origin isolated. On GitHub Pages, which cannot set response headers, the playground gets this from coi-serviceworker; a relay serving the page sets Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy itself. Certificate trust. A WebSocket has no certificate-error interstitial to click through: either the browser already trusts the certificate, or the connection fails.
data.3-network-model-l4-flows-not-l3-packets#:
The containers’ sockets use the WasmEdge socket extension in the module wasi_snapshot_preview1, as github.com/stealthrocket/net imports it: sock_open, sock_bind, sock_listen, sock_connect, sock_recv_from, sock_send_to, sock_getaddrinfo, sock_shutdown, plus sock_getsockopt, sock_setsockopt, sock_getlocaladdr and sock_getpeeraddr. Its socket types are SOCK_STREAM and SOCK_DGRAM only; there is no raw socket. The engine therefore sees a container connecting to 10.42.2.2:80, never a packet.
The alternative is what container2wasm does: an L3 network stack based on gVisor’s netstack (c2w-net, built on gvisor-tap-vsock) that carries Ethernet frames, forwarded over WebSocket in its delegate=ws://... mode.
L4 flows (chosen) L3 packets (gVisor netstack) Fits the socket ABI directly: one host call is one flow operation needs a TCP/IP stack between the ABI and the wire Firewall sees connect, listen, port, peer: what a rule names must reassemble flows from packets to say the same Cost one frame per write TCP inside the container’s stack, carried over the relay’s TCP: TCP over TCP, retransmission on two levels, per-packet framing Size in the browser none beyond the driver a whole network stack compiled into the engine UDP datagram frames native ICMP / ping not expressible by the ABI (see below) possible, but gvisor-tap-vsock says ICMP is not forwarded outside its network Decision: L4. Addressing is still IP-shaped, because the lab teaches it:
one network per class, default 10.42.0.0/16; student n gets 10.42.n.0/24, the teacher 10.42.0.0/24; the relay allocates every address (as Neutron allocates fixed_ips), the browser never chooses one; DNS: ..class resolves to the container’s address, through sock_getaddrinfo, answered by the relay; a container’s bare name still resolves inside its own browser; TCP: listen registers the address and port at the relay; connect is a request to the relay, which checks the rules and opens a stream to the listener’s browser, or refuses (the caller gets ECONNREFUSED, or a timeout if the teacher chose “drop” for teaching); UDP: each sock_send_to is one datagram frame with a source and destination, at most 8 KiB; the relay checks it and forwards or drops it. Ping. The ABI cannot send ICMP, so ping is taught through a small extension the engine provides later (M-relay-5): an import module wctr_net with one function, icmp_echo(addr, seq, payload), which the driver turns into an echo frame. The relay answers it on behalf of the destination port if its rules allow ICMP echo ingress (protocol: icmp, port_range_min: 8, type 8). A ping image built against it gives the expected pedagogy: allowed, the student sees replies; removed, the pings time out, and the flow log shows the drop.
The Neutron API reference defines a security group rule by direction (ingress or egress), ethertype (IPv4 or IPv6), protocol (tcp, udp, icmp, …, or any), port_range_min and port_range_max (for ICMP: the ICMP type and code), and one of remote_ip_prefix, remote_group_id or remote_address_group_id. A security group has a stateful flag: a stateless group “bypasses connection tracking”, so both directions of a flow need rules. Nova’s guide states the overall policy: “Security groups deny everything by default, so rules indicate what is allowed”, and adding a rule is additive. A port carries security_groups, fixed_ips, port_security_enabled (“security group rules and anti-spoofing rules are applied”) and allowed_address_pairs. Neutron creates, for each project’s default group, four rules (all IPv4/IPv6 egress, and ingress from ports in the same group), and for other new groups only the two egress rules; a template of those rules is configurable (used_in_default_sg, used_in_non_default_sg, remote_group_id: PARENT). Quotas count security_group and security_group_rule per project.
data.6-security-audit#6. Security audit:
The relay is a network service on a LAN full of untrusted clients, parsing their frames. Every row is a requirement for the implementation and a test.
Threat Mitigation A student impersonates another (identity, address) Session token bound to the session; ports and addresses assigned by the relay; source addresses in frames ignored and rewritten; a port id in a frame must belong to the session (Neutron’s anti-spoofing, without allowed_address_pairs). A student claims another’s DNS name Names are ..class, the label fixed by the relay at Join; label collisions get a suffix. Display names injected into the dashboard Display names are data: length-limited (40), control characters removed, escaped by the dashboard; the label is derived, ASCII. Brute-forcing the class code 10 characters from 32 symbols (50 bits); Join rate-limited per source IP (5 per minute) and per class; the code expires with the class or on rotation. Flooding and resource exhaustion Per session: 256 open streams, 64 listeners, 32 pending connects, 10 ports, token buckets on frames per second (2 000) and bytes per second (2 MiB/s, burst 8 MiB), all configurable by the teacher. Per connection: 1 MiB of buffered data. Global: a cap on sessions (port quota) and on unauthenticated connections (32, 10 s to authenticate). Oversized or malformed frames WebSocket read limit of 16 KiB + header per message; a frame whose length disagrees with the message is a protocol error that closes the connection; every decoder fuzzed (go test -fuzz, corpus committed). Slow readers (memory held) Credit-based windows; a stream with no credit for 60 s is reset; WebSocket ping every 15 s, close after 45 s without a pong. A malicious public page attacks the relay through a student’s browser Every API call and the WebSocket need a token in a header or in the first frame, never a cookie, so no ambient authority exists to ride (no CSRF). The WebSocket upgrade, and CORS on the few calls a page makes, check Origin against the relay’s own origin and the --cors-origin allowlist, which is empty by default and never * (relay v0.3.0). The Host header must be one of the relay’s names or addresses (DNS rebinding). Local Network Access prompts are a second barrier, not the first. The admin API reachable from the LAN Off by default: the admin side listens on the Unix socket and loopback only; --admin-listen is explicit and can require mTLS. Secrets Admin token, CA key and token-signing key: 0600 files under os.UserConfigDir(), never in a URL, a command line, an environment variable or a log; logs redact anything token-shaped. Join links carry the code and the certificate hash in the URL fragment. The CA is name-constrained. A compromised relay It sees all classroom traffic by design. It runs as the teacher’s user, needs no privilege (port 8443), and holds no credential beyond its own. Supply chain govulncheck in CI; dependencies limited to connect-go, protobuf, a WebSocket library and, later, quic-go/webtransport-go (which implements draft-16 of WebTransport over HTTP/3, not an RFC: pinned and re-checked when the draft moves).
data.7-performance#7. Performance:
Budget. The relay must not be what limits a lab. The assumptions to measure, not results:
40 students on one access point share its airtime; a lab’s traffic is small (HTTP requests, a database query, a chat), a few hundred kB/s per student, so the aggregate stays far below what one Go process forwards; container-to-container round trip ≈ two Wi-Fi round trips (A to relay, relay to B) plus the relay’s processing, which must stay under 1 ms at the 99th percentile; framing cost: our 10-byte header, the WebSocket header (2 to 10 bytes, plus a 4-byte masking key from client to server, RFC 6455) and the TLS record: under 0.3 % for a full 16 KiB frame, significant only for very small writes, which the engine coalesces within one event-loop turn; head-of-line blocking on the single TCP connection is the main latency risk on a lossy Wi-Fi; WebTransport’s independent streams are the remedy. What to measure, against what.
Measure Reference Target relay forwarding throughput, one core, 16 KiB frames a direct TCP connection between the same two processes on loopback at least 50 % of it relay frames per second, one core, 64-byte frames the same reported, then optimised added latency per hop (p50, p99) at 40 sessions × 10 streams direct loopback TCP p99 < 1 ms memory per idle session none < 64 KiB rule evaluation per connect, 500 rules linear scan constant per flow after the first lookup, indexed by protocol and port end to end in a real classroom (40 browsers) the same lab with all containers in one browser reported Measurements follow the fleet’s rule: interleaved rounds, single core, never on a loaded machine. Masking and unmasking WebSocket payloads is a byte loop on the hot path: it goes to a shared SIMD kernel (go-simd) if it shows in the profile, not into the relay.
data.alternatives-considered#Alternatives con:
Before writing the relay, existing overlay networks were evaluated (October 2026) against what a lab needs: running in a browser tab with nothing installed, inside the engine’s Go js/wasm, a firewall the teacher controls, flow logs, a LAN mode without internet, and high availability.

With end-to-end WireGuard, the relay sees nothing: good for privacy, but there is no relay-side enforcement and no relay-side flow log. Filtering at the receiver is sound against untrusted students (a student can only weaken their own node), but egress rules cannot be enforced on a node the student controls, and logs kept by the endpoints can be forged by the student whose flows they describe. The relay-side log is the lesson. Neutron’s model only partly translates to Tailscale ACLs: ingress rules map to tags and ports; egress rules and stateless groups do not. headscale has no HA, so adopting it would not remove the Raft work. A 26 MB WireGuard + netstack per tab, against a socket-level relay that adds no network stack to the engine (performance of both is unmeasured). Decision: hybrid (option C). Our relay stays the classroom data plane and firewall; identity and certificates come from go-authn; client failover follows DERP’s ordered-relay pattern. A later option, not planned: tsnet in the teacher’s relay to reach native machines on an existing tailnet.
data.authentication-and-authorization#Authent: Principal Credential Can Teacher (local) the Unix socket, mode 0600, or the admin token over loopback everything Teacher (dashboard on another machine) the admin token, as Authorization: Bearer, over TLS; opt-in with --admin-listen everything Student a session token from Join own ports, own flow decisions, read the groups that apply to them The admin token is 256 random bits generated by wctr-relay init, stored 0600 under os.UserConfigDir(), compared in constant time, never printed except by an explicit wctr-relay token show, never in a URL. The class code (10 characters, from an alphabet without look-alikes) is shown on the teacher’s screen and in a QR code. Join exchanges it with a display name for a session token: signed by the relay (Ed25519), bound to the class and the session id, valid 12 hours, revoked by KickSession or by rotating the code. mTLS is not used for students: provisioning client certificates into 40 browsers is the problem the class code solves. A teacher may require mTLS on --admin-listen. Authorization is checked in the handler from the token’s claims, never from a field of the request (a student cannot pass another session’s id).
data.chaos-cases#Chaos cases: Fault Expected behaviour A student reloads the page The page reconnects with its session token; within a 120 s grace period the relay keeps the session’s ports and addresses; open streams are reset (the container sees a connection reset, as after a network cut); listeners are re-registered by the engine. The teacher’s laptop sleeps Every WebSocket drops. On wake, browsers reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter (1 s to 30 s), so 40 browsers do not reconnect in the same millisecond; sessions older than the grace period are re-joined silently with the token. The relay restarts or crashes Classes, sessions, groups, rules, ports and address allocations are persisted (written to a temporary file, then renamed) after every change; tokens stay valid because the signing key is on disk. Flows do not survive: they are reset and logged as such. Clock skew between machines Tokens are checked against the relay’s clock only; the browser’s clock is never trusted. Wi-Fi loss Detected by the ping/pong timeout, handled as a reload. Mixed versions (page and relay) The first frame carries a protocol version; the relay refuses an unknown major version with a message the page shows. In deployment (b), skew cannot happen. Two teachers’ relays on one LAN Each class has its own code, certificate and CA; a join link names one relay. The chaos campaign (M-relay-5) injects these faults into a test classroom of real browsers and records what breaks.
data.data-plane-framing#Data plane framing:
One WebSocket per browser, binary messages, one frame per message:
0 1 2 6 10 +------+------+--------------+--------------+----------------+ | type | flags| stream id | length | payload ... | | u8 | u8 | u32 BE | u32 BE | <= 16 KiB | +------+------+--------------+--------------+----------------+ Frame types (version 1, numbered in the protocol): HELLO, WELCOME, ATTACH, ATTACHED, DETACH, LISTEN, LISTENING, UNLISTEN, CONNECT, ACCEPT, REFUSE, DATA, WINDOW, CLOSE, RESET, DATAGRAM, RESOLVE, RESOLVED, RESULT, REAUTH, GOAWAY; ECHO comes with ICMP in M-relay-5. The client allocates odd stream ids and the relay even ones. The session token is checked before the WebSocket upgrade: a browser cannot set an Authorization header on a WebSocket, so the token travels as a second subprotocol (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: wctr-relay.v1, bearer.) — a header, never a URL. REAUTH hands the relay a fresh token on the open connection. Control payloads are protobuf messages from the same .proto; DATA payloads are raw bytes. Flow control is credit-based per stream (64 KiB initial window, WINDOW frames return credit) and per connection (1 MiB), so one fast sender cannot fill the relay’s memory for a slow reader. The relay rewrites every source address: a frame names a stream or a port the session owns, never an address the browser chose.

data.decisions#Decisions:
# Question Decision 1 Browser to relay transport WebSocket over TLS (wss), one per browser, multiplexing every container’s flows. WebTransport is the second transport, added later. WebRTC is not used. 2 Where the page comes from Both paths are first-class: the relay serves the playground itself over HTTPS on the LAN, and the page on GitHub Pages connects to the relay. Whether a school can install a CA is not known in advance, so the join flow detects which works (see Join-flow detection). 2b Where the TLS certificate comes from In this order: (1) a publicly trusted certificate from ACME through go-authn/servercert (a school-owned name such as class. pointing at the relay; DNS-01 for a LAN-only relay is to be added to servercert); (2) the relay’s internal CA, whose root a school installs; (3) WebTransport certificate hashes from the GitHub Pages page. Caddy in front of the relay is the documented alternative. 3 Network model L4 flows: the relay brokers connect/listen/datagrams between container endpoints, each with a virtual IP and a DNS name. No packet-level (L3) network stack in the engine. 4 Firewall model Neutron’s networks, ports, security groups and rules, allow-only, stateful by default, enforced at both ends of every flow, with flow logs. 5 Control API gRPC services, served with Connect so the same handler answers gRPC, gRPC-Web and Connect; the teacher’s CLI is a separate cobra binary, wctr-relay. 6 Identity The relay assigns every address; nothing a browser sends about its own identity is trusted. Teacher: an admin token. Students: a class code exchanged for a short-lived session token. 7 Internet mode The same relay can run on the internet for remote or hybrid students, with OpenID Connect sign-in verified by go-authn/oidc, logins through go-authn/rp, and go-authn/bridge as the identity provider for SAML-only universities. The LAN mode keeps working with a class code and no identity provider. 8 High availability The control plane (classes, groups, rules, addresses, signing keys, audit) is replicated with Raft across relays; the data plane (live flows, connection tracking) is not. One relay holds a class at a time, under a lease with an increasing epoch; clients follow an ordered list of relays and refuse an older epoch. 9 Build or adopt Hybrid: our relay stays the classroom data plane and firewall (relay-side enforcement and flow logs are the lesson); go-authn supplies identity and certificates; the client failover follows Tailscale’s DERP pattern. See Alternatives considered. 10 Seeing the network The relay serves a live flow map: a go-widgets page (Go js/wasm on a canvas) fed by an aggregated, coalesced server stream over the Connect protocol; denied flows flash red with the refusing decision; teacher view of the class, per-student view of one’s own flows. See The live flow map. Answers to the questions this page first left open (decided 2026-10-26):

Opening flows is part of the lab. Neutron’s default group is a template the teacher can choose. Can schools install a classroom CA? Unknown per school, so both TLS paths stay first-class and the join flow detects which works IPv6 later; the model carries ethertype, the first milestones allocate IPv4 only The teacher’s containers they join as a session (subnet 0, label teacher), so the teacher can publish shared services The docs repository has no ADR convention, so these tables are the decision record.
data.flow-logs#Flow logs: Every decision can be logged: time, class, source and destination session, port, address and port, protocol, verdict (allow, deny, revoked), the matching rule or no rule, and at close the bytes each way and duration. Rules carry a log flag; denies are always logged. The teacher streams logs live (CLI, dashboard); a student sees the decisions about their own ports, which is the point of the exercise (“why can’t I reach Bob’s server?”).
data.high-availability#High availability:
The problem. A class runs on relays in a datacenter; if that relay stops answering, the class must move to another one without losing its setup.
What state exists.
Plane State On failover control classes, join codes, members and their identities’ hashes, security groups and rules, port and address/DNS assignments, session-token signing keys, audit log replicated: survives data live streams, UDP connection tracking, listeners not replicated: flows are reset (containers see ECONNRESET, which is teachable); listeners are re-registered by the engines when they reconnect; addresses, names and rules are the same Replication: Raft, not a CRDT. The control plane is a replicated state machine (the Raft paper, §2: servers “compute identical copies of the same state” and are “fully functional (available) as long as any majority of the servers are operational”; “they do not depend on timing to ensure the consistency of the logs”). Security rules need that linearizability. A CRDT (go-crdt exists in the fleet) merges concurrent updates instead of ordering them: an add-wins set would bring back an allow-rule the teacher deleted on another replica during a partition. A deleted allow-rule must never reappear by merge, so CRDTs are the wrong tool here. The library candidate is etcd’s raft (the core algorithm only: “the application supplies its own network transport and persistent storage”; Apache-2.0; used by etcd, CockroachDB and TiDB). The relay already reaches its state through a Store interface (FileStore on a single relay), which the replicated store implements.
One relay per class: an epoch lease. The star needs a class to live on one relay at a time. The replicated store holds, per class, a lease (relay_id, epoch, expiry); a relay takes or renews it through the log, and each new holder increments the epoch (Raft’s terms are the model: “terms act as a logical clock”, and a server rejects a request with a stale term). The epoch is in Welcome and in Class; a client refuses a relay that shows an older epoch than one it has seen (fencing), so a partitioned old holder cannot keep half a class. A relay that cannot renew its lease stops serving the class before the lease expires, with a margin for clock drift.
Quorum. A majority quorum of 2 datacenters does not survive the loss of either (2 of 2 needed). Three sites are needed: two datacenters and a small witness (a third voter that serves no class). The trade-off is written down rather than hidden: without the witness, a two-site deployment is active/passive with manual failover.
Client-side failover, after DERP. Tailscale’s DERP documentation describes the pattern: each client gets a map of relays, picks one by latency, “selects the next closest region” when its region is unreachable, and saves the list so it works while the coordination server is down. Ours: the join link carries a signed class descriptor listing the relays in order (not DNS-only failover: resolvers cache past a TTL). A client health-checks, reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter, and resumes with its session token, valid on any relay of the cluster (signing keys are in the replicated store and rotated through it; OpenID Connect tokens stay valid because issuer and audience are the cluster’s). Each relay has its own certificate from servercert.
Phase 2: federation. Relay-to-relay links would let one class span relays (geographic proximity, partial failure), the firewall still enforced at both ends. Not before the single-holder design is shipped and measured.
Chaos plan (M-relay-HA): kill the lease holder in the middle of a lab; partition one datacenter; skew the clocks of the lease holder; run mixed relay versions during a rolling upgrade; make every student reconnect at once (thundering herd: jitter, and admission control that answers “retry after” rather than accepting more than it can serve).
data.internet-mode-openid-connect#Internet mo:
The same star can run on a server on the internet, for remote or hybrid classes. It must then not be open to everyone, so it signs people in with OpenID Connect, using the fleet’s own libraries:
Piece Library What it does here verifying tokens go-authn/oidc the relay verifies the token that comes with Join, RefreshSession and the teacher’s calls: issuer compared exactly, audience required, expiry required, an allowlist of signature algorithms (no none, no HMAC), key-set refetches bounded. With Type: "at+jwt" it refuses an ID token presented as an access token (RFC 9068 §4, which the library cites). logging people in go-authn/rp the browser login (authorization code with PKCE S256, state and nonce) and the teacher’s wctr-relay login, a loopback login (RFC 8252) that listens on 127.0.0.1 only and opens the system browser universities go-authn/bridge an OpenID provider in front of a SAML federation: people “log in at their own university, through RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN”. The recommended identity provider for academia, since many university IdPs speak SAML only. Authorization model.
Issuer and audience pinned in the relay’s configuration (--oidc-issuer, --oidc-audience); one issuer per relay. Class membership: an identity alone admits nobody. A student still joins a class with its join code; the class may also list who may join — sub:, email: (only an address the issuer marked verified: go-authn/oidc’s Username falls back to email only when email_verified is true, for the same reason) or group: — and may require an identity (--require-identity), which a relay on the internet sets on every class. Teacher role: a configured group claim (--teacher-group) gives the admin role, but only on the admin listener, never on the public one. One identity, one session per class: joining again returns the same session (same addresses), and the per-session quotas are therefore per identity, not per IP address — a class behind one NAT is not one student. Long connections and short tokens. A data connection lasts a lesson; an access token lasts minutes. The relay’s own session token is what the data connection holds, bound to the session; before it expires the page calls RefreshSession (with a fresh OIDC token, from the refresh grant go-authn/rp handles) and sends the new session token in a REAUTH frame. No flow is dropped. A connection whose token expires without REAUTH gets GOAWAY and closes. Logout and revocation: the teacher’s KickSession, or deleting the class, ends the session and its tokens at once (the relay checks that the session exists on every authentication, not only the signature).
Internet hardening.
Authenticate before upgrading: the session token is checked before the WebSocket upgrade, and before any per-session state is allocated; an unauthenticated request costs a header parse and a signature check. Per-IP limits before authentication: token buckets on Join and on upgrade attempts per source address, and a cap on concurrent unauthenticated handshakes. ReadHeaderTimeout (5 s), MaxHeaderBytes (16 KiB) and idle timeouts against slowloris. Max sessions per identity (one per class) and per class (its subnets). Frame and flow bounds as on the LAN (security audit). No admin API on the public listener: the admin API stays on the Unix socket and loopback, or on a separate --admin-listen that requires the teacher role (or the admin token). Audit log (JSON lines, 0600): logins, refusals, kicks, class and rule changes, with pseudonymous identities. Privacy (GDPR). Students are data subjects, often minors. The relay stores, per session: a display name the student typed, a derived DNS label, and — with OpenID Connect — a pseudonymous identifier (a hash of issuer and subject), never the token, the e-mail address or the groups (they are checked at the moment of joining and dropped). Flow logs hold addresses and ports, not contents. Retention: everything about a class is deleted with the class (wctr-relay class delete); the audit log is pruned after 30 days by default (--audit-retention). The teacher’s institution is the controller and should say so in the course’s information notice.
data.join-flow-detection#Join-flow detection:
The join link (printed and shown as a QR code by wctr-relay class create) carries, in its URL fragment (never sent to a server): the relay’s LAN URL, its GitHub Pages fallback, the join code, and the WebTransport certificate hash when there is one. The page:
fetches https:///v1/info (a small public JSON document: version, relay id, TLS mode) with a 3 s timeout; if it answers, the certificate is trusted (public ACME or an installed internal CA) and the browser is sent to the playground served by the relay (deployment (b)); otherwise, if the page is on GitHub Pages and the browser has WebTransport with serverCertificateHashes, it connects with the hash (deployment (a)); otherwise it tells the student exactly what is missing (install the CA, accept the Local Network Access prompt, or use another browser), rather than failing silently. Whether a page loaded after a certificate warning is still a secure context in each browser is not established by the references opened here; M-relay-3 measures it in the three browsers before any path relies on a click-through.

data.policy-and-evaluation#Policy and evaluat: Default deny. A flow is allowed only if a rule allows it. Both ends. A flow from port S to port D is allowed iff S’s egress rules allow it and D’s ingress rules allow it, as Neutron filters at each port. Order-free. Rules only allow, groups on a port are a union, so there is no order to get wrong: the result is the same whatever order rules were added in. The decision names the rule that allowed it, or “no rule” if none did. Default groups. Each class gets a default group with Neutron’s four rules (egress allowed, ingress from the same group), and the teacher can switch the class template to isolated (egress only to the teacher’s subnet, no ingress), which is the better start for a lesson on opening ports. remote_group_id matches the current addresses of every port in that group, so a rule “ingress tcp 5432 from group web” follows containers as students start and stop them.
data.quotas#Quotas: Per class, as Neutron’s: security_group (default 50), security_group_rule (default 500), and port (default 40 × 10). Per session, for safety rather than pedagogy: see the security audit.

data.services#Services:
The control API is gRPC, described in one .proto; the relay serves it with connect-go, whose handlers support gRPC, gRPC-Web and the Connect protocol and mount on a plain net/http server. The Connect protocol uses no HTTP trailers and supports server streaming over HTTP/1.1 (bidirectional streaming needs HTTP/2), so a browser dashboard can call the same API, including the live flow log, without a proxy. Nothing in the API needs bidirectional streaming.

data.statefulness#Statefulness:
Statefulness is connection tracking of L4 flows, which the relay has for free because it brokers every flow:
TCP (stateful group): the rules are checked once, at connect; the stream then carries both directions until either side closes. UDP (stateful group): an allowed datagram creates a conntrack entry keyed by the 5-tuple; replies match it; it expires after 30 s without traffic. Stateless group: for TCP, the reverse direction (D’s egress, S’s ingress) must be allowed too, or the connect is refused; for UDP, every datagram is checked both ways. This is Neutron’s “two rules for a TCP flow”, visible to students. Rule changes: after any change, the relay re-evaluates open flows and resets the ones no longer allowed, logging them as revoked. A firewall that silently keeps old connections confuses a lesson.
data.the-engines-networkdriver#The engine’s N:
The engine maps the socket host functions onto a driver; the in-browser network it has today becomes the local driver, and the relay is a second one:
// Package netdriver, in go-wasmcontainers/engine (planned). type NetworkDriver interface { // Attach gives a container an endpoint on a network; the driver // assigns its address and DNS name. Attach(ctx context.Context, c ContainerRef, network string) (Endpoint, error) Close() error } type Endpoint interface { Addr() netip.Addr Listen(ctx context.Context, network string, port uint16) (net.Listener, error) // "tcp" Dial(ctx context.Context, network string, addr netip.AddrPort) (net.Conn, error) // "tcp", "udp" ListenPacket(ctx context.Context, network string, port uint16) (net.PacketConn, error) // "udp" Resolve(ctx context.Context, name string) ([]netip.Addr, error) Detach() error } The engine owns this interface; the relay’s client library implements it, so native engines (wazero) and browser engines use the same driver code, and the relay’s tests need no browser.
data.the-live-flow-map#The live flow map:
The relay serves a page that draws the class’s network as it happens: nodes are sessions (the students and the teacher) holding their containers, coloured by security group; edges are live flows, their width following throughput; denied flows flash red with the rule decision that refused them (“no ingress rule of bob/web allows tcp/80”), because seeing the refusal is the lesson.
Data. The page calls a server-streaming RPC, FlowLogService.WatchFlowMap, over the Connect protocol (the reason connect-go was chosen: “the other RPC types also support HTTP/1.1”, server streaming included, so a browser needs no proxy). The relay aggregates: every tick (default 4 Hz) it sends one update holding the per-edge counters (src port → dst port, protocol and port: bytes each way, flows opened, open, denied) and the discrete events since the last tick (opened, closed, denied, revoked, with the rule ids). A slow page gets coalesced updates — the newest state replaces the unsent one — never an unbounded queue. A view is capped (400 nodes, 2 000 edges; past that the update says what was left out). View. A stable, incremental layout, not a force simulation (no full relayout per tick): sessions are boxes on a grid ordered by subnet (teacher first), containers inside them, so a node does not move when traffic changes and 40 students × several containers stay readable on a projector. Click a node or an edge for its details (groups, the rules that matched, conntrack state, counters). Filters by student, group and port. Light and dark themes. Pause and replay of the last minutes are deferred (the ring of the last 1 000 events is already kept). Technique (decided 2026-10-26): the fleet’s own toolkit. The page is a Go js/wasm application built on go-widgets/toolkit and run in a by go-widgets/webcanvas, which blits “an RGBA framebuffer into the canvas and routes DOM pointer and keyboard events back into the scene”. The widgets a flow map needs and the toolkit lacks — a node-link graph view with groups, animated edges and incremental layout, a legend, a filter bar, a detail panel, a sparkline — are added to go-widgets, generic and reusable, under its conventions (MVVM, Theme, keyboard navigation, its coverage gate), each in its own pull request and minor release; the relay imports them. Everything is served by the relay (same origin, the .wasm included), under a strict Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' (the narrowest allowance WebAssembly compilation needs), no inline script, no third-party request — the relay runs without internet. The join QR code is drawn from go-gfx/qr’s module matrix. Because a canvas has no DOM to assert on, the page’s tests read the view model (MVVM’s testable layer), which the page exposes to the test harness. Access. The teacher’s view of the whole class needs the admin role (the admin token on loopback or the Unix socket, or the OpenID Connect teacher role in internet mode). A student may open their own view: only the flows that touch their own containers, with the other end named but no flow between two other students — the privacy between students the class needs. Tests. Playwright (Chromium and Firefox) drives real flows through an in-process relay and asserts what the page’s view model says (edges present, a denied flash with its rule, counters moving), not screenshots; the update latency from a flow to the screen, the frame time at about 200 nodes and 1 000 edges on one core, and the relay’s CPU at 40 sessions are measured.
data.the-problem#The problem:
A teacher has a laptop on the classroom LAN, possibly with no internet access. Ten to forty students each open the playground in their own browser (Chrome, Firefox or Safari, sometimes on a school-managed machine). Each browser runs WASI containers in Web Workers. Inside one browser, containers already share a virtual network. The lab now needs student A’s container to reach student B’s container, for example a web server on one side and curl on the other, and the teacher needs to decide and show which flows are allowed, the way a cloud’s security groups do.
The answer on this page: every browser opens one secure WebSocket to a relay that runs on the teacher’s laptop. The relay brokers socket-level (L4) flows between containers, and it is also a firewall: every flow is checked against security groups whose model is OpenStack Neutron’s. The teacher manages them through a gRPC control API. The brief called it the “c-api”; this page reads that as control API (the control plane, as opposed to the data plane that carries the containers’ bytes).
data.the-teachers-command-line#The teacher’s:
A separate binary, wctr-relay, in its own repository (go-wasmcontainers/relay), built with cobra like the rest of the fleet. It is the relay daemon and its client, as wctrd and wctr are for the engine, but in one binary because a teacher installs one thing. It stays out of wctr, whose surface is compatible with the Docker Engine API and is what students learn.
wctr-relay init # classroom CA, admin token, state directory wctr-relay serve [--listen :8443] [--admin-listen 127.0.0.1:8444] wctr-relay class create "Networking 101" # prints the join link and QR code wctr-relay class sessions | kick wctr-relay sg list | create [--stateless] | delete wctr-relay rule add --ingress --proto tcp --port 80 --remote-group web wctr-relay rule del wctr-relay port list [--student alice] | set --sg web,db wctr-relay flows [--follow] [--deny-only] [--student alice] wctr-relay explain alice/web bob/curl tcp/80 wctr-relay ca export | ca rotate

data.two-deployments#Two deployments: (a) Page on GitHub Pages, relay on the LAN (b) Relay serves the page over HTTPS Works without internet no (the page and its assets come from GitHub Pages) yes Local Network Access prompt yes, on every student browser; may be blocked by policy no (same origin, same address space) Cross-origin isolation coi-serviceworker response headers, no service worker Certificate WebTransport hashes (no trust needed), or a trusted certificate for wss a certificate every student browser trusts Version skew page and relay released separately the relay embeds one playground release: no skew Both are first-class. Whether a school can install a CA on its machines is not known in advance, so neither deployment is a fallback for the other.
data.where-rules-are-enforced#Where rules are: Between browsers, at the relay: it is authoritative. Inside one browser, the engine applies the same rules, pushed by the relay with the session, so that a lesson works the same with two containers of one student. That copy is advisory: a student who modifies their own page only affects their own containers, which they control anyway.
data.where-the-certificate-comes-from-in-orde:
A publicly trusted certificate from ACME. A school-owned name (say class.example-school.fr) resolves to the relay’s address — a private LAN address is fine — and a public CA issues its certificate: no student installs anything. Caddy’s automatic-HTTPS documentation states the key point for a LAN-only relay: with the DNS challenge, “the server requesting a certificate does not need to be externally accessible”; it needs credentials for the DNS provider. The DNS-01 challenge (RFC 8555 §8.4) proves control of the name with a TXT record at _acme-challenge. whose value is the base64url SHA-256 of the key authorization. The relay takes its certificate from go-authn/servercert, the fleet’s shared source of TLS server certificates: files reloaded on change, or ACME through autocert with External Account Binding. servercert answers tls-alpn-01 and http-01 only (“No dns-01”), which covers a relay on the internet; it also covers a LAN-only relay whose organisation has a GÉANT TCS / HARICA account with pre-validated domains, which issues “with no ACME challenge at all”. For every other LAN-only relay, DNS-01 is added to servercert (shared code, not a copy in the relay). An IP-address certificate is not an option for a LAN relay: Let’s Encrypt issues them (generally available since 15 January 2026, short-lived profile only, 160 hours), but servercert refuses IP names, and whether a public CA would validate a private LAN address was not established here; a name is the path. The relay’s internal CA, when no name or no internet at issuance is available. wctr-relay init creates a root (ECDSA P-256), name-constrained to the classroom’s names and addresses, which a school installs on managed machines by the same policy channel that installs any CA. mkcert’s README states the risk of any such CA: its key “gives complete power to intercept secure requests” from a machine that trusts it — hence the name constraints, a 0600 key that is never exported, and wctr-relay ca rotate. Caddy’s internal issuer is the same idea (a local CA it tries to add to the system trust store, which “isn’t guaranteed to work” without privileges), but it lives in Caddy’s PKI app, not in CertMagic (which has no internal issuer), so embedding it would mean embedding Caddy. WebTransport certificate hashes from the GitHub Pages page (deployment (a)): no trust needed, under the constraints of §1. Caddy as a front is the documented alternative for a teacher who already runs it: wctr-relay serve --tls off --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 (the relay refuses --tls off on any non-loopback address) behind Caddy’s reverse_proxy, with Caddy’s own ACME or tls internal and caddy trust. The relay still checks Origin and Host itself. If on-demand TLS is used it “must be both enabled and restricted” (Caddy’s words), with an ask endpoint.
Secrets: a DNS provider’s API token, an EAB HMAC key and the CA key are read from files (0600, owned by the relay’s user), never from a command line, an environment variable or a URL.

data.does-anything-work-with-existing-docker-: The API is meant to be compatible with the Docker Engine API (v1.47 is the reference the code is written against), so a client of that API can be pointed at /var/run/wctr.sock. Only the subset M1 needs is planned first; see the roadmap.
data.not-ctr#Not ctr: ctr is the command line that containerd ships. Trainees meet it on Kubernetes nodes, where it means something different, so a lab teaching a ctr of its own would teach the wrong tool in the place they will use it.
data.not-docker#Not docker: Docker is a product and a trademark of another organisation. This engine is not Docker and does not ship under its name: it is compatible with the Docker Engine API, which is a statement of compatibility and nothing more. That is why its socket is /var/run/wctr.sock and the address variable is WCTR_HOST.
data.why-wctr#Why wctr?: wctr is the command line and wctrd the daemon that serves it. The name follows the convention of the container tools that came before it, ctr, nerdctl and crictl: a short name ending in ctr, for container. The w is for wasm: wctr reads as wasm container, and says that this is the WebAssembly variant.
