go-wasmcontainers/gpu is the module for GPU access from WASI containers: wasi-nn inference, wasi:webgpu compute and rendering, on WebGPU in the browser and on the CPU natively. Pure Go. The design and its references are in docs/DESIGN.md.
Status (v0.6.0): inference, compute, rendering and surface input exist.
Part State onnx: ONNX model loader and CPU operators done (v0.1.0) nn: wasi-nn host module (wasi_ephemeral_nn), CPU backend; wasinn Go guest bindings; the mnist example done (v0.2.0) nn/webgpu: wasi-nn on the GPU, WGSL kernels (browser) done (v0.3.0) wasi:webgpu compute (host and Go guest), examples/compute done (v0.4.0) rendering: wasi-gfx:surface and surface-webgpu, frames to the page, examples/triangle done (v0.5.0); the dashboard (v0.6.0) shows the frames in its Surfaces view surface input: on-pointer-up/down/move and on-key-up/down streams for the guest, webgpu.SurfaceInput for the page done (v0.6.0); the dashboard forwards pane events since its v0.8.0 on-resize and on-frame streams, vertex buffers, depth-stencil not yet A container asks for the GPU with wctr run --gpu (engine v0.13.0 or later). The execution target is checked: gpu needs that capability and a GPU backend, and otherwise fails with unsupported_operation, never running on the CPU in its place. A process without --gpu gets no adapter.
data.onnx#onnx: The ONNX loader runs a model on the CPU. Operators: Add, AveragePool, Concat, Constant, Conv, Div, Dropout (inference), Flatten, Gemm, Identity, MatMul, MaxPool, Mul, Relu, Reshape, Softmax, Sub and Transpose (default domain, operator sets 7 and later, float tensors, int64 for shapes). A model using anything else fails at load, naming every unsupported operator. The model is untrusted input: its sizes and the work of one inference are bounded, and the decoder is fuzzed. CPU performance has not been measured yet.
data.rendering-surfaces#Rendering: surfaces:
In the browser each wasi-gfx:surface is an OffscreenCanvas in the engine’s worker; present turns it into an ImageBitmap handed to the page, which draws it (in the playground, a dashboard pane). The page acknowledges each frame: at most two are unacknowledged, a page that stops acknowledging slows the guest to a frame per second without stopping it, frames are paced to 60 per second, and surfaces are at most 1920×1080. Render pipelines take their vertices from the shader (no vertex buffers yet) and have no depth-stencil. Surface input (v0.6.0): pointer and key events reach the guest as wasi-gfx:surface streams, which the host serves for core modules per the Canonical ABI. The page’s events are untrusted and bounded: finite coordinates up to 2^16, key text of at most 64 bytes of valid UTF-8, 256 queued events per stream and 64 streams per surface.
examples/triangle draws a spinning triangle. On an Apple Metal adapter, the end to end test checks 60 frames in order, the clear colour, the triangle, frames that change, and a rate within the pacing (one run: 51 frames per second).
Testing on headless Linux (fixed in v0.5.1). Before v0.5.1, on Linux headless Chromium 143 with SwiftShader (the CI fallback lane), every frame reached the page fully transparent. Headless Linux Chromium can back a WebGPU canvas only with Skia on Vulkan: launch it with --enable-features=Vulkan --use-vulkan=swiftshader --use-angle=swiftshader (or a real Vulkan driver); otherwise the WebGPU instance is torn down at the first canvas configure and frames are blank. With those flags the Linux SwiftShader lane passes the same checks as macOS, pixels included, and the pixel checks are strict. go run ./internal/cmd/gpuprobe --canvas follows one canvas frame from the GPU to the page, to check a browser.
data.wasi-nn-on-the-cpu-and-on-webgpu#wasi-nn:
wasinn gives Go guests Load, NewContext, SetInputF32, Compute and OutputF32. In the browser, each ONNX node becomes one WGSL compute dispatch on a WebGPU device of the graph’s own. The WGSL kernels are checked twice: natively, against all 122 vendored ONNX node tests, with each kernel’s index arithmetic run in Go (no GPU needed); and in a browser, on the real WGSL. On an Apple Metal adapter (Chromium 143), 123 of 123 pass, MNIST-12 within 3.1e-5 of the reference. CI has a macOS lane that must get a GPU adapter or fail, so the GPU path is proven on a real Apple GPU; the Linux lane runs on SwiftShader, a software adapter, and is labelled as proving the WGSL and not a GPU.
The playground has an mnist image that runs wasi-nn in the browser.
data.wasiwebgpu-compute#wasi:webgpu compute:
Containers are WASI preview 1 core modules and the engine has no component-model runtime, so the gpu module parses the WIT and implements the Canonical ABI for a 32-bit memory by hand. The host serves every function of the wasi:webgpu interface; in the browser it maps them to WebGPU in the engine’s worker. Quotas per process: 4096 handles, 256 MiB of buffers, 1 MiB per WGSL module and 256 pipelines; a submission still running after 2 seconds has its device destroyed, and fallback adapters are refused.
On an Apple Metal adapter, examples/compute (adding two 1M-float vectors, multiplying two 256×256 matrices) matches the CPU on every element, with the matmul in 15 ms on the GPU against 42 ms on the guest’s CPU, and the vector add in 69 ms against 3.5 ms (dominated by transfers). That is one run, not a benchmark.

data.engine#Engine:
Engine v0.30.0 does not have:
CPU accounting: a WebAssembly guest gives none, so wctr stats shows CPU as --; host-path volumes: only named volumes exist, and a host path is refused; signals: processes are the WASIX subset, a child is stopped only with its container, and Ctrl-C in a terminal erases the line (a container’s first process has its own stdin and terminal since v0.30.0: run -it, attach); published ports in the browser (-p works natively since v0.22.0; in the browser it is in progress, through a second origin, with the groundwork portmap.Virtual in v0.24.0; natively there is no SCTP, and the source address the guest sees is its own). A container on several networks binds to its primary address or to all (0.0.0.0), not to a secondary address alone; aliases work on in-engine networks only; no IPv6 on in-engine networks; the DNS shadows a container’s own UDP server on port 53 at the resolver addresses (see Networking); a Kubernetes API, and volume drivers or tmpfs; a distinct quota error: when a container exhausts its storage quota, the write surfaces to the module as EIO. wctr build runs shell-form RUN from engine v0.17.0 on the shell base image (shell v0.1.0, ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell:0.1.0, public). See Build and Shell.
data.playground#Playground:
The playground (v0.4.1, built on engine v0.30.0) takes one wctr command per line, with no pipes in that line. It has exec, a shell (the shell image), typing into exec -i, and run -it and start -ai (its end-to-end test runs wctr run --rm -it shell). Its dashboard is v0.6.0, so GPU panes do not send input there yet. There is no -p in the browser yet: the second origin for containers’ pages is deployed, but the rest of it is in progress and not live. Networks stay inside the page: no Internet, no published ports. Ctrl-C stops waiting for a container but leaves it running. Each container is bounded: 256 MiB of memory, a 5-minute run, 64 MiB of writes, 4 MiB of logs, and 64 containers at once.
The default UI, the dashboard, makes the page slower to be ready than the terminal page (728 ms against 1070 ms in Chromium on the live site), because dashboard.wasm was 20.45 MB raw (5.32 MB gzipped) when measured; dashboard v0.4.2 made it smaller and no newer figure has been measured. The terminal-only page is at ?ui=terminal.

data:
Containers have a network (engine v0.10.0, extended in v0.14.0). Networking is live in the playground since playground v0.3.0 (engine v0.10.0 there), and joining a teacher’s class from the page works.
$ wctr network create lab $ wctr run -d --name web --network lab netprobe serve 80 $ wctr run --rm --network lab netprobe get http://web/class The second container reaches web by its name, through the network’s DNS.
data.a-class-network#A class network: wctrd --relay URL --relay-join-code-file FILE [--relay-ca CA] [--relay-network class] joins a class of the relay and adds a network on which containers get the class’s addresses and names, under the teacher’s firewall. The join code is read from a file, which is refused if other users can read it; the session token is kept with mode 0600 and refreshed. Since engine v0.11.0 a host can also add and remove such a network at run time, which is what the playground’s “Join class” does.
data.dns-by-container-name#DNS by container n: Every network has a DNS server inside the engine, on UDP port 53, answering on 127.0.0.11, 127.0.0.1 and ::1. It answers A and AAAA for the names on the network and NXDOMAIN for anything else; nothing is forwarded outside. Guests built with -tags getaddrinfo resolve through sock_getaddrinfo instead.
data.in-the-browser#In the browser:
In the playground, nothing leaves the page: there is no route to the Internet or to the machine. Measured by net bench (200 sequential GETs, then one 8 MiB GET, between two containers on the bridge) on an Apple M4 Max, under a load of 16 to 19, so indicative only:
latency p50 / p90 throughput Chromium (the page) 1.1 / 1.4 ms 106–112 MB/s native: the same engine on wazero 0.33 / 0.39 ms 1.2 GB/s native: Go net/http over loopback TCP (upper bound) 0.05 / 0.07 ms 3.8 GB/s The browser is about 3 times slower in latency and 11 times in throughput than the same engine natively, because every socket read or write is a WASI call that crosses from the container’s worker to the engine’s. Larger reads per call are an open item.
data.limitations#Limitations: -p is not in the browser yet (in progress, through a second origin); natively it exists since engine v0.22.0 (see above). A container on several networks binds to its primary address or to all of them (0.0.0.0), not to a secondary address alone. Aliases work on in-engine networks only; no IPv6 on in-engine networks; no AF_UNIX. The DNS shadows a container’s own UDP server on port 53 at those resolver addresses, and an unconnected UDP sendto to the resolver is not answered.
data.networks#Networks: The default network is bridge (10.88.0.0/16); the other is none, which gives no sockets. wctr network create|ls|inspect|rm|connect|disconnect|prune, and wctr run --network NAME; the container’s address is shown by inspect. The API has /networks. Since v0.14.0: wctr run --network-alias NAME gives a container more names on a user-defined network (replicas may share one); wctr network connect [--alias NAME] NETWORK CONTAINER attaches a running container at once, so a container can be on several networks; disconnect [-f] detaches it; and prune [-f] [--filter label=K[=V]] removes unused networks. Lists can be filtered by label, and wctr events has network events (create, connect, disconnect, destroy, prune).
data.published-ports-engine-v0220-native#Publ:
$ wctr run -d --name web -p 8080:80 netprobe serve 80 $ wctr port web 80/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8080 A container has no socket on the host, so a published port is a listener that wctrd opens on the host and proxies into the container (the way Docker’s userland proxy does, not iptables). UDP keeps one session per client, ended after 90 seconds of silence. The API shapes are Docker’s (HostConfig.PortBindings, PublishAllPorts, Config.ExposedPorts, NetworkSettings.Ports).
A binding without an address listens on 127.0.0.1, not on every address as Docker does. -p 8080:80 makes the container reachable from this machine only; -p 0.0.0.0:8080:80 makes it reachable from the network. A host port someone holds refuses the start (Bind for 127.0.0.1:8080 failed: port is already allocated), and nothing of that container is left listening. A container on --network none cannot publish. Bounds: each binding proxies at most 128 connections and 256 UDP clients at a time, and at most 1024 bindings per container; the parsers are fuzzed. No SCTP, and the source address the guest sees is its own, not the client’s. In the browser, -p is not available yet: it is in progress, through a second origin (the host would be the page, not a machine). Engine v0.24.0 adds the groundwork, portmap.Virtual, published ports with no sockets, for an engine that runs in a page.
data.sockets-for-guests#Sockets for guests: A guest opens sockets with the WasmEdge socket extension of wasi_snapshot_preview1 (its V2 form, as stealthrocket/wasi-go serves it) and preview 1’s sock_* calls. A stock Go program that uses github.com/stealthrocket/net v0.2.1 runs unchanged: HTTP and UDP between containers, by container name.
data.the-wasi-host#The WASI host: wctrd --wasi engine is the default, because sockets need it. wctrd --wasi wazero gives no network.

data: https://go-wasmcontainers.github.io/playground/ is a dashboard of WASI containers, images and volumes with a terminal running wctr, in a web page. There is no server: the engine runs in the page (the browser executor, runtime/browser, new in engine v0.2.0). This is playground v0.4.1, on engine v0.30.0.
data.completion-and-editing#Completion and ed:
The terminal completes with Tab, as a shell does: subcommands, flags, -m sizes, local images (for run and rmi), the catalogue of images to pull, container names and IDs (logs, rm, inspect, and only running containers for kill) and image arguments. Editing is bash-style: Up and Down for the history, Ctrl-R to search it, Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E, Ctrl-B and Ctrl-F to move, Ctrl-U, Ctrl-K and Ctrl-W to cut, Ctrl-D, and Ctrl-L to clear. The history is kept per tab (in sessionStorage). From a keypress to the line on screen took 7 to 14 ms in Chromium and 23 ms in Firefox, measured in CI.
The line editor and its completion are the package cli/lineedit of the engine: pure Go, usable by anyone who embeds the engine’s CLI.
data.images#Images: Image What it is hello, greet the small demonstration modules lab a module with subcommands: echo, env, pwd, ls, cat, write, count, sleep, spin, hog, bench, fs, exit, esc net a networking probe: serve, get, bench, udp-echo, udp, lookup, dial mnist classifies a handwritten digit with wasi-nn every pkgx wasip1/wasm bottle: 7 images from 6 bottles today (age, go-md2man, shfmt, lua, luac, sqlite3, minigzip) derived from pkgx’s signed catalogue at build time, see below
data.limits-per-container#Limits per containe: 256 MiB of memory, a 5-minute run, 64 MiB of writes, 4 MiB of logs, and 64 containers at once.
data.not-yet#Not yet: One wctr command per line (pipes need the shell image’s sh); the dashboard in the page is v0.6.0, so GPU panes send no input yet; no -p published ports in the browser (in progress, through a second origin that is deployed; natively -p works since engine v0.22.0). Networks stay inside the page: there is no route to the Internet. Ctrl-C stops waiting for a container but leaves it running. See Limitations and the roadmap.
data.offline-and-updates#Offline and updates: The playground works offline (dashboard.wasm is in the service-worker cache). A new version installs in the background and applies when you choose “Reload to update”. Only one tab runs the engine at a time; another tab can take over with “Use it here”. The engine was ready in 130–190 ms on a first visit in Chromium, 80–115 ms after a reload, and 75 ms offline.
data.pkgx-images-are-derived-not-listed#pkgx:
The site build (cmd/site build --pkgx) reads pkgx’s signed wasip1/wasm catalogue (go-pkgx.dev/catalog; the signature is verified) and mirrors the newest version of every project that has one published. No list is typed in the playground: a bottle published tomorrow is an image after the next build, and wctr images and the dashboard’s Images view show whatever catalog.json holds, each entry with its project, version and layer size.
Version: the highest by numeric components, then rebuild counter, then raw string; the catalogue’s order is not trusted. Names: one image per name in the project’s provides that has a bin/.wasm (lua gives lua and luac); all of a bottle’s images share its layer. When no provides name has a module, the bottle’s modules are the images (zlib gives minigzip). A name taken by two projects goes to the one whose last path segment equals it, else the smallest project name; the other is published as -. Dependencies are ignored: a wasip1 module is statically linked. Limits: 400 projects, 900 images, 8 images per bottle, 100 MiB per compressed layer, 512 MiB and 20 000 entries unpacked, 3 minutes for the catalogue and 30 in all. An unverifiable or empty catalogue stops the build; there is no built-in list. A bottle over a limit, or whose tar has an absolute path, a .. or a link leaving the root, is refused and listed in findings.json. Page cost: one catalog.json of about 330 bytes per image, read once; an image’s blobs are fetched only when a command uses it. Smoke test: CI runs every derived image with --version and --help (or a named probe such as lua -v) under the engine and under wasmtime and compares exit status, stdout and stderr byte for byte; a failure or difference that is not named, with its reason, fails the job. Lua’s errors, which use WebAssembly exception handling, work in Chromium, Firefox and natively. The first lua run took 69–108 ms in Chromium and 170 ms in Firefox, measured in CI.
Images and pulls survive a reload: they are kept in the browser’s IndexedDB. So do the containers (engine v0.4.0): state, exit code, logs and written files. A container that was running comes back exited with code 137, and a --rm one is removed.
data.speed#Speed: Measured in one CI run, the page is ready in 0.46 s in Chromium and 1.0 s in Firefox, and the first hello runs in 81 ms and 291 ms. Cold start is slower than wasmtime (23 ms natively). The table is on Performance.
Engine v0.30.0: run -i/-t, attach and start -ai in the page. A line whose own wctr flags say -i (run, start, exec; also -dit) gets what you type; the end-to-end test runs wctr run --rm -it shell and exec -it c sh and checks the exit status. The usercontent shell forgets requests the playground never answers (shell.js and sw.js): a pending-request leak fixed.
The dashboard is the main UI: the dashboard (Containers, Images, Volumes, Networks, Terminal) runs on the persistent engine worker. The terminal alone, on xterm.js, stays at ?ui=terminal. Networking in the browser: containers talk over TCP and UDP, by name (see Networking). The net image has serve, get, bench, udp-echo, udp, lookup and dial. Join class: with a teacher’s relay, the page joins the class network (the dashboard’s Networks view, Join class…). The relay must run with --cors-origin https://go-wasmcontainers.github.io (relay v0.3.0 or later). The join code is typed in a password field, posted once to the engine worker, and never stored. wasi-nn in the browser: the mnist image reads a handwritten digit (see GPU). It still works offline and keeps its images and containers across a reload.
GPU surfaces and compute: the compute and triangle images (copies of gpu v0.5.1’s examples) run with --gpu; a surface is a pane under the dashboard’s Surfaces view. A container without --gpu, or a browser without WebGPU, gets no adapter: these images print no GPU adapter and exit 2. WASIX: programs started by a shell run as WASIX processes in the page. The shell image, ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell:0.1.0, mirrored verbatim and pinned by its digest: wctr run --rm shell sh -c 'echo a | cat' and wctr exec -it CONTAINER sh work in the page. Typing into exec -i: a line whose own wctr flags say -i gets what you type, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D included. wctr build and wctr compose are wired into the page’s wctr, as in cmd/wctr. The shell of a second origin for containers’ pages (https://go-wasmcontainers-usercontent.github.io/) and the route policy: the first half of -p in the browser. -p is not live yet.
data.what-you-can-type#What you can type:
wctr pull, run, ps, logs, rm, rmi, images, inspect and kill, start, stop, restart, diff, stats, events, volume, network and system df|prune, plus help and clear. run takes --rm, -d, --name, -e, -w, -m, --entrypoint, -v NAME:/path[:ro] and --network NAME. Exit codes are the native engine’s: the container’s own, or 125, 126, 127, 134 and 137; see Commands.
$ wctr run --rm hello $ wctr run --rm -e NAME=you greet

Every behaviour of the engine that follows an external format or protocol is written against one of the documents below. The engine repository’s own docs/REFERENCES.md says, for each, which version was opened and which file it governs.
Reference What it decides OCI Image Format Specification (v1.1.1) digests, manifests, image indexes, image config, layers and whiteouts, image layout OCI Distribution Specification pulling manifests and blobs from a registry Docker Registry token authentication the bearer-token challenge and token request Docker Engine API (v1.47) the endpoints and schemas wctrd is compatible with Wasm OCI artifact layout (CNCF TAG-Runtime) media types and config fields of a Wasm image wazero (v1.12.0) the runtime, its WASI preview1 imports and writable filesystem interface WASI preview1 the system interface a wasip1 module is written against

wctr-relay connects the WASI containers of a class’s browsers (or engines) through one relay that is also a firewall, with security groups modelled on OpenStack Neutron. It runs on the teacher’s laptop for a classroom LAN, or on a server for remote students with OpenID Connect sign-in. Release v0.2.0 of go-wasmcontainers/relay covers milestones M-relay-1, M-relay-2 and M-relay-2b (the live flow map) of the design.
What works today: the relay, its firewall, its control API, the wctr-relay command and the live flow map, tested natively and, for the flow map, in Chromium and Firefox. The engine does not use the relay yet (its network driver is being written), so containers in the playground cannot reach each other through it yet.
data.certificates#Certificates:
Students’ browsers must trust the relay’s certificate. In order of preference:
a publicly trusted certificate for a name the school owns: --tls acme --acme-domain class.example-school.fr (ACME through go-authn/servercert), or --tls files --cert … --key …; the relay’s internal CA (the default, --tls internal): install the root printed by wctr-relay ca export on the class’s machines; it is name-constrained to the relay’s names and addresses; behind Caddy or another TLS proxy: --tls off --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 (refused on any other address).
data.install#Install:
Download the binary for your system from the releases (it includes the flow map), or build it:
go install github.com/go-wasmcontainers/relay/cmd/wctr-relay@v0.2.0 # without the flow map page Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0; Linux, macOS and Windows.
data.pages#Pages: Command reference The live flow map Security model
data.start-a-class-teacher#Start a class (tea:
wctr-relay init --name relay.local --ip 192.168.1.10 # state directory, admin token, internal CA wctr-relay serve --listen :8443 & wctr-relay class create "Networking 101" # prints the class id and the join code Students join with the code. Each gets a subnet (10.42..0/24), each container an address and the name ..class. A new class starts isolated: no ingress, egress to the teacher’s subnet only. Opening flows is the lab:
wctr-relay sg create web --class wctr-relay rule add web --class --ingress --proto tcp --port 80 wctr-relay rule add default --class --egress --proto tcp --port 80 wctr-relay port set alice/web --class --sg default,web wctr-relay flows --class --follow # every allow and deny, with the rule that decided wctr-relay explain --class bob/curl alice/web tcp/80 Deleting a rule resets, at once, the flows only that rule allowed.

data:
wctr-relay is one binary: serve runs the relay; every other command is a client of its control API. Locally they use the state directory’s admin socket (0600: its permissions are the credential); for a remote relay, --server URL --token-file FILE [--ca-file ROOT.pem], where URL is the relay’s --admin-listen address over https (the token is never a flag value). --state-dir (default /wctr-relay) applies to all, and so does --admin-socket PATH (since v0.2.1): the admin socket’s path, admin.sock in the state directory by default. A Unix socket path holds at most 103 bytes on macOS and 107 on Linux; a longer one is refused with that reason, so a deep state directory needs a short --admin-socket, given to serve and to the other commands alike.
Command What init [--name N] [--ip A] create the state directory (0700): admin token, session-token signing keys, and the internal CA for those names and addresses serve run the relay class create NAME a class; flags --cidr (default 10.42.0.0/16), --session-bits (24), --domain (class), --template isolated|neutron, --allow sub:…|email:…|group:…, --require-identity class list classes and their join codes class sessions CLASS sessions: label, name, subnet, connected class kick CLASS SESSION end a session: its connection, ports and tokens class rotate-code CLASS a new join code; the old one stops admitting class delete CLASS delete the class and what the relay knows of its students sg list --class C groups and their rules sg create NAME --class C [--stateless] [--description D] an empty group (it allows nothing) sg delete GROUP --class C a group no port uses rule add GROUP --class C --ingress|--egress [--proto tcp|udp|icmp|any] [--port 80|8000-8080] [--remote-ip PREFIX|--remote-group G] allow a flow rule delete RULE --class C remove a rule; the flows only it allowed are reset port list --class C [--student S] ports: name, address, groups port set PORT --class C [--sg a,b] [--port-security on|off] a port’s groups (replaces the list) flows --class C [--follow] [--deny-only] [--student S] [--backlog N] the flow log explain --class C SRC DST PROTO/PORT what the firewall would decide, and which rules ca export, ca fingerprint, ca rotate [--name] [--ip] the internal CA teacher-session --class C --out FILE a session token (written 0600) for the teacher’s own containers flowmap --class C --url URL (the relay’s https address) the link to the class’s live flow map, with a read-only 12-hour ticket in its fragment (v0.2.0) version the version A port is named by its id, its DNS name (web.alice.class) or student/container (alice/web).
data.serve-flags#serve flags: Flag Default What --listen :8443 the address students reach (data plane /v1/data, join, /v1/info) --tls internal internal, files, acme, or off (loopback only) --cert, --key PEM files for --tls files, re-read when they change --acme-domain, --acme-email, --acme-directory, --acme-cache ACME for --tls acme (default CA: Let’s Encrypt) --eab-kid, --eab-hmac-file External Account Binding (the HMAC key in a 0600 file) --acme-http also answer http-01 on this address (e.g. :80) --cors-origin none a browser origin (scheme://host[:port]) allowed besides the relay’s own, e.g. the playground’s (on GitHub Pages); repeatable, never *. See Browsers on another origin --host Host names served; any other is refused --oidc-issuer, --oidc-audience, --oidc-type OpenID Connect token verification --teacher-group groups-claim value granting the teacher role on --admin-listen --admin-listen also serve the admin API on this address (TLS) --session-ttl 12h session token lifetime --audit-retention 720h how long the audit log keeps events --relay-id host name this relay’s id

data.getting-a-binary-that-has-it#Getting a b:
The page’s WebAssembly is about 5 MB, so it is not in the repository: the binaries attached to each release carry it. From source:
go run ./internal/buildflowmap go install -tags flowmap ./cmd/wctr-relay A plain go install …@latest serves the page, which then says the map is missing from that build.
data.how-it-works#How it works:
The relay aggregates its flow log per edge — source container, destination container, protocol and port — and streams one update per tick (4 per second) over FlowLogService.WatchFlowMap, a server stream of the Connect protocol. A slow page gets the newest map, never a backlog. An update holds at most 400 containers, 2 000 flows and 200 events.
The page is a Go WebAssembly application built on go-widgets’ GraphView (a node-link graph over a view model, added to go-widgets for this page and reusable elsewhere) and LogView. The relay serves it itself, under a strict Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; connect-src 'self' — no inline script, nothing loaded from anywhere else, so it works on a classroom LAN with no internet.
data.not-yet#Not yet: Pause and replay of the last minutes; the relay keeps the last 1 000 events, the page shows the last 200.
data.who-can-see-what#Who can see what: Viewer Credential Sees The teacher the link from wctr-relay flowmap: a read-only ticket in the URL fragment (never sent to a server, removed from the address bar when the page loads), valid 12 hours the whole class A student their own session token (#class=…&session=…) only the flows that touch their own containers, and the containers at the other end The ticket allows watching that class’s map and nothing else: it cannot change a rule, list the groups, or join the class.

data.browsers-on-another-origin-cors#Browsers:
The playground runs on GitHub Pages and calls Join and RefreshSession on the relay from the browser. That is a cross-origin request, so the browser first sends a preflight, and the relay answers it only for the origins it is told to trust:
wctr-relay serve --cors-origin https://go-wasmcontainers.github.io An allowlist, empty by default. The relay’s own origin is always allowed. Add a page’s origin once per origin (scheme://host[:port], the flag can be repeated). * and wildcards are refused. Without the flag, a page served from elsewhere cannot join this relay. Only the calls a page needs: Join, RefreshSession, WatchFlowMap, WatchFlows and ListPorts. Other public calls answer no preflight, and the admin listener has no CORS at all. Exactly the headers Connect needs. The method and header lists are those of connectrpc.com/cors, plus Authorization, Wctr-Session, Wctr-Map-Ticket and User-Agent. Firefox lists User-Agent in the preflight because Connect-Web sets it. Preflights are cached for 2 hours. No credentials mode. Tokens travel in headers and never in cookies, so the browser has nothing to attach on its own, and the relay never sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. The data WebSocket checks the same list. Browsers do not preflight WebSockets, so a hostile page could otherwise open the data channel with a token it had obtained (cross-site WebSocket hijacking). The relay therefore refuses an upgrade whose Origin is not on the list. A client that is not a browser sends no Origin and is unaffected. The --cors-origin flag appeared in relay v0.3.0. It replaces --origin, which covered only the WebSocket and allowed the Pages host by default.
data.principals#Principals: Who Credential Where May Teacher, on the relay’s machine the admin socket (0600 in a 0700 state directory) Unix socket everything Teacher, remote the admin token (Authorization: Bearer) or an OpenID Connect token carrying --teacher-group --admin-listen only, over TLS everything Student a session token from Join (join code, plus an OpenID Connect identity when the class requires one) --listen their own ports and flow decisions; read the groups The public listener never grants the teacher role, whatever arrives on it (the admin token included).
data.secrets#Secrets: The admin token, the signing keys, the CA key, an EAB key and the state file are 0600 files of the relay’s user, refused if anyone else can read them, never on a command line, in an environment variable or in a URL. The internal CA is name-constrained: even its key cannot sign for another site.
data.tested#Tested: Every point above has a test in the repository; the decoders of untrusted input (frames, tokens, join codes, labels, rule specifications, and the relay fed arbitrary frames) are fuzzed in CI, and govulncheck runs on every change.
data.what-the-relay-keeps-about-students#What: Per session: the display name typed, a derived DNS label, and — with OpenID Connect — a pseudonymous hash of issuer and subject (never the token, the e-mail address or the groups, which are checked at join time and dropped). Flow logs hold addresses and ports, not contents. Deleting a class deletes all of it; the audit log (logins, refusals, kicks, rule changes) keeps 30 days by default. The teacher’s institution is the controller under the GDPR.
data.what-the-relay-refuses#What the relay re: Identity is the relay’s: it assigns every address and port; a frame that names a port the session does not own is refused, a datagram from a source port the sender has not bound is dropped. Authentication before the upgrade: the session token is a WebSocket subprotocol (bearer.), checked before the upgrade and before any per-session state; it never appears in a URL. An Origin that is neither the relay’s own nor in --cors-origin, and an unknown Host, are refused. Pre-authentication limits per source address on joins and upgrades, a cap on concurrent handshakes, header timeouts and sizes. Bounds: 16 KiB frames, 64 KiB stream windows, and per session: 256 streams, 64 listeners, 10 ports, 32 pending connects, 2 MiB/s and 2 000 frames/s; a connection whose send queue passes 4 MiB is closed. Per class: 50 security groups and 500 rules (Neutron’s quotas). A frame that does not decode, data beyond the window, or a frame out of place closes the connection. Tokens: Ed25519, one fixed layout and one algorithm, checked against the relay’s clock; a kicked session’s tokens stop working at once.

A POSIX shell for WASI containers, in pure Go, built for GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm: go-wasmcontainers/shell. It is what makes shell-form commands work: RUN a && b in a Containerfile, wctr run IMAGE sh -c '…', and wctr exec -it CONTAINER sh.
A WebAssembly module cannot start another program: Go’s port has no fork or exec, and WASI preview 1 has no process calls. So the shell uses a small subset of WASIX, in WASIX’s own import module (wasix_32v1): proc_spawn3, proc_join, fd_pipe, proc_id, proc_parent, tty_get and tty_set, and nothing else (no fork, exec, threads or signals). The engine serves that subset from v0.17.0 (wctrd --wasi engine, the default): see Architecture.
Status: shell v0.3.0 is released. v0.3.0 updates its dependencies: coreutils v0.5.0, then the coreutils commit that adds env CMD, xargs and find -exec (released as coreutils v0.6.0), and engine v0.29.2 (typed-ahead keys survive the switch to raw mode, which the line editor relies on). v0.2.0 added a line editor on a terminal (arrow keys, history, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-D) and made wasix a module of its own (github.com/go-wasmcontainers/shell/wasix, tag wasix/v0.1.0) with wasix/exec, which mirrors os/exec for WASI containers. sh runs on the engine, where pipelines through the coreutils work. The current base image is ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell:0.3.0 (also tagged latest), built by the release workflow of shell v0.3.0 and pushed with manifest digest sha256:bc3b16b7ef328e8e7a2f30e93f2e14456b7119c7d674d156914038ee38c5c5ec (wasip1/wasm, one layer of 59 entries): sh with the line editor, /bin/coreutils.wasm (the multicall module of wasmdesk/coreutils) with its tools as symbolic links, a root-only /etc/passwd, and the config Shell ["/bin/sh","-c"], which is what a shell-form RUN runs. It carries coreutils at the commit released as v0.6.0 (shell v0.3.0’s go.mod requires the pseudo-version v0.5.1-0.20261031200158-fe13df492e30), so env CMD, xargs and find -exec run in it; the shell agent’s pull test runs ls, xargs and find -exec against it. Earlier images stay available: shell:0.2.0 (coreutils v0.4.0, 51 entries, digest sha256:32bb0127…505a7) and shell:0.1.0 (shell v0.1.0, 42 tools), which is the one some examples elsewhere in these pages use. The images are public; pull the current one with:
$ wctr pull ghcr.io/go-wasmcontainers/shell:0.3.0 wasix: //go:wasmimport bindings for the subset, with a Go API; a module of its own since wasix/v0.1.0. wasix/exec: os/exec for WASI containers (Command, Cmd, Start, Wait, Run, Output, CombinedOutput, the stdin, stdout and stderr pipes, ExitError, LookPath). It has no Kill or CommandContext, because signals are not in the WASIX subset. sh starts its children through it. sh: the mvdan.cc/sh v3.14.1 interpreter (patched with one change: a pipe function, since upstream’s os.Pipe is ENOSYS on wasip1), whose external commands start with proc_spawn3. sh does pipelines, redirections, here-documents, command substitution, cd, exported variables, $?, set -e/-u/-x/-f/-a, exec, sh -c, sh file and an interactive prompt on a TTY, with a line editor since v0.2.0. Coreutils v0.6.0 adds env CMD, xargs and find -exec (programs run through wasix/exec on wasip1 and os/exec natively). Coreutils v0.5.0 (the image :0.2.0 carries v0.4.0, :0.3.0 v0.6.0) brought grep flags (-F -r -l -c -o -q -w -H -h, combined flags, POSIX exit 2), a tee that writes its files as the input arrives, POSIX ls FILE, find expressions, sort keys, head and tail (-c, +N, tail -f), date +FORMAT, tr and a full POSIX printf, and adds hostname, uname, id, whoami, clear and which. By design of the subset it has no signals, no job control and no process substitution.
